opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that we're still in a phase where the form factor is being driven more by imagination than by the task. When people say "humanoid," they picture something that looks like us: two legs, two arms, five-fingered hands, a head with cameras where the eyes would be. And there's a real argument for that. The world is built for human bodies, so a human-shaped robot can in principle use our doors, our tools, our workstations. But "in principle" is doing a lot of work there.

Look at where the hardware actually is. The legs have gotten very good, partly because reinforcement learning in simulation transfers well to locomotion. You can see robots doing flips and dancing. But locomotion isn't where most of the economic value is. The value is in manipulation, in the hands and the arms, and that's where the configuration is clearly unfinished. Dexterous hands are still fragile, expensive, and hard to maintain. Tactile sensing is primitive compared with human skin. The degrees of freedom often don't match what the control policies can actually use. So you get a body that looks complete from the outside, but the parts that matter most are the least mature.

There's also a mismatch between body and brain. The configuration should co-evolve with the model controlling it. Right now a lot of teams design the hardware first and then try to train a policy on it, and the data they collect is tied to that specific body. Change the hand, change the joint layout, and much of your data loses value. That's a sign we haven't converged. In a mature industry you'd have a few dominant designs, like the car settling on four wheels and a steering wheel. We're nowhere near that.

And practically, a lot of real deployments may not need legs at all. A wheeled base with a capable upper body might cover most factory and household tasks more cheaply and safely. So I'd say the humanoid configuration is unfinished in three ways: the hands aren't good enough, the body and the learning system aren't designed together yet, and we haven't really decided which parts of the human form are essential and which are just familiar. Until those questions get answered by real usage data rather than demos, the form will keep changing.

r001.rationale: The response points to robots doing flips and dancing, then contrasts that visible locomotion with immature hands and manipulation. This communicates that demonstrations showcase mobility more than manipulation.

r002.rationale: It says locomotion has advanced while manipulation remains unfinished, and that the industry has not converged on a dominant design. Together, these communicate a lack of a settled configuration combining both capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say the honest answer is that we haven't actually agreed on what a humanoid robot is for yet, and the hardware reflects that confusion.

Look at what's shipping right now. Most of these machines are built around the idea that if it looks like a person, it can do what a person does. But a human body isn't a design spec, it's an evolutionary compromise. We have two legs because of how we ended up walking out of trees, not because bipedal locomotion is the optimal way to move a payload through a warehouse. So when you copy the form without asking what the form is actually buying you, you inherit all the costs and only some of the benefits.

The second problem is the hands. Everyone talks about legs because walking is dramatic on a demo video, but the economically valuable part of a human is the hand, and we're nowhere close. A real hand has something like twenty-odd degrees of freedom, tactile sensing across the whole surface, and it's compliant in a way that lets you grab an egg or a wrench without switching modes. Most robot hands today are either strong and dumb or delicate and fragile. Until that's solved, the "humanoid" is really a very expensive mobile base carrying two gripper arms, and you could get there with a much simpler body.

Third, the configuration is not complete because the data loop isn't closed. The body and the brain are being designed separately. Companies build the hardware, then try to collect teleoperation data on it, then train a policy, then discover the hardware can't do what the policy wants. The right way, I think, is to co-design them, which means the body you build in year one is almost certainly the wrong body for the model you have in year three. So any configuration today is provisional by definition.

And the last piece is the boring stuff: battery life, cost of actuators, maintenance. A robot that works for ninety minutes and then charges for two hours isn't a worker, it's a prototype. The form factor conversations tend to skip over that, but it's the thing that decides whether anyone actually deploys these.

So when I say they're not complete, I don't mean we need one more joint or a better sensor. I mean the whole stack is still searching for its shape. The humanoid form is a bet that generality is worth the cost. I think that bet might be right eventually, but the current configurations are the first draft of it, not the answer.

r001.rationale: The response says walking is dramatic in demo videos and contrasts that attention with the economically valuable hand, indicating demonstrations emphasize mobility over manipulation.

r002.rationale: It discusses incomplete hands, costly mobility, and configurations still searching for their shape, but does not clearly state that the cause is a lack of convergence on a configuration combining strong mobility and strong manipulation.

astra-6.text:
I think today’s humanoid robots have the basic shape, but the capabilities aren’t yet integrated. Having two arms and two legs doesn’t automatically give a robot the ability to work in a human environment. It needs to perceive what’s happening, maintain balance, handle objects, and adjust when something unexpected occurs—all at the same time.

Take something as simple as picking up a cup. The robot has to judge where it can grip, apply the right force, and respond if the cup slips. A configuration that performs one carefully rehearsed task may still struggle with that kind of variation. So when I say the configuration isn’t complete, I mean the body, sensing, and control still need to develop together into a reliable system.

r001.rationale: It discusses handling objects and mobility-related capabilities together, but does not say demonstrations emphasize mobility more than manipulation.

r002.rationale: It says body, sensing, and control need to develop together, but does not identify a lack of convergence on a configuration combining strong mobility with strong manipulation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is what we mean by “complete.” A robot can have a head, two arms, and two legs and still lack the abilities needed to function reliably in everyday life. The shape alone isn’t enough.

The hands need to manipulate objects, the body needs to maintain balance, and perception needs to guide action as the environment changes. Those capabilities have to work together. If a robot performs a task only under carefully arranged conditions, there’s still a gap between that demonstration and a useful humanoid.

So I wouldn’t say there’s one final configuration we already know we’re missing. We need to understand the tasks first, then develop the body and its intelligence together.

r001.rationale: The response discusses manipulation and balance but does not say humanoid demonstrations emphasize mobility more than manipulation.

r002.rationale: It says there is no known final configuration and calls for developing body and intelligence around tasks, but does not attribute incompleteness to a lack of convergence on a configuration combining strong mobility and manipulation.
